To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the light emitted from III-V semiconductor devices under high electric field bias is due to hot-carrier-induced direct interband transitions and cannot be described as a black-body emission.

hot-carrier light emission in GaAs devices is due to both direct interband and intersubband optical transitions and that it is not possible to extract the 'carrier temperature' from the measured spectra.
hot carrier induced light emission is made up by radiative interband and intraband transitions, the latter being more pronounced for higher electric fields.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the optical properties of III-V semiconductor devices under high-bias and high-current-density operation.

the development and application of a self-consistent Monte-Carlo (MC) and pseudopotential (PP) simulation technique for the investigation of hot-carrier induced light emission (HCL) in semiconductor devices.

the development of a theoretical model for hot-carrier-induced luminescence in GaAs devices that is based on self-consistent Monte-Carlo simulations of carrier transport and a pseudopotential calculation of the direct radiative optical transitions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hot carrier light emission is not a simple black body emission from a 'carrier temperature'.
the observed light emission is not a simple signature of hot carriers.
the light emission from hot carriers is a complex phenomenon that is not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hot-carrier-induced luminescence spectra are a result of the combined effects of the carrier heating, the band structure, and the bandgap renormalization.
hot-carrier-induced electroluminescence (HC-EL) in III-V semiconductors is a very rich and complicated phenomenon.
the light emission in GaAs devices is a very complex process and the results of the simulations can be understood only in a qualitative manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the carrier distributions are highly nonthermal, and that this nonthermality is reflected in the spectra.
hot-carrier-induced electroluminescence is not a single process but a combination of different processes.
the carrier distribution function is a much more useful tool for the description of hot carrier phenomena than the carrier 'temperature'.
